chapters.file: ch12 - Seeing Soldiers, Seeing Persons Wittgenstein, Film Theory, and Charlie Chaplin’s Shoulder Arms.md
chapters.relation: Hilsabeck argues that Wittgenstein's notion of aspect perception ("seeing as") is not a phenomenology of illusion, as film theorists like Allen and Turvey take it, but an ethical matter of articulating experience within forms of life and language games. He reads Chaplin's Shoulder Arms through this lens: Doughboy's tree-disguise gag and his repurposing of war objects (Limburger cheese as grenade, gramophone horn as snorkel) demonstrate imaginative, ethical vision, while the German soldier who cannot see the tree-as-man exhibits "aspect blindness." The film makes viewers' willingness to "see anew" a test of attunement and mutual acknowledgment, casting the environment of WWI trench warfare and mechanized shock as what stifles this imaginative seeing.

chapters.file: ch13 - Part 2. War as Condition of Self-Formation and Self-Dissolution.md
ch14 - Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity.md
chapters.relation: Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.

chapters.file: ch15 - The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty.md
chapters.relation: Burgoyne argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty places the violated body at the center of its rendering of the War on Terror, using somatic intensity and affective experience against Steven Shaviro's reading of the film as pure, affect-draining proceduralism. He traces Maya's arc from witness to coercive agent through the torture of Ammar, the Goya-like montage of interrogation videos, and the suicide-bomb killing of her friend Jessica, mapping the film onto Sarah Cole's poles of disenchanted violence (the raw, exposed flesh of the interrogations) and enchanted violence (the technologically choreographed, almost magical SEAL raid on Abbottabad, likened to Baudrillardian simulated combat). The closing unzipping of bin Laden's body bag deflates any triumph into embodied ambiguity.

chapters.file: ch16 - “All in War with Time” Medium as Meditation in Sherman’s March.md
chapters.relation: Rhu reads Ross McElwee's Sherman's March—ostensibly a documentary about Sherman's Civil War campaign but really about a heartbroken filmmaker's search for love amid Cold War nuclear dread—through Walker Percy's The Last Gentleman and Stanley Cavell's The World Viewed. He shows how the film enacts Cavell's ontology of film (viewing the world "from behind the self," movies as reliefs from private fantasy) and the dialogue between perfectionism and skepticism Cavell draws from Emerson's "Experience" and Nietzsche and Kierkegaard. McElwee's deliberately unpolished, self-conscious "personal documentary"—stumbling on the riverbank, leaving in his own second thoughts—turns the war film into a meditation on consciousness, mediation, and being "all in war with Time."

chapters.file: ch17 - The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki.md
chapters.relation: Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.

chapters.file: ch18 - Part 3. The Ethical Tribulations of War.md
ch19 - The Ubiquitous Absence of the Enemy in Contemporary Israeli War Films.md
chapters.relation: Pötzsch uses cognitive film theory (Murray Smith's alignment and allegiance, paradigm scenarios and schemata) to argue that Beaufort, Waltz with Bashir, and Lebanon, though hailed as antiwar films, covertly reinforce a militarist "scopic regime" through the "ubiquitously absent enemy." Formal devices—the tank scope's tunnel vision in Lebanon, shot/reverse-shot and voice-over confined to Israeli soldiers, the animated flashbacks of Waltz with Bashir—align and ally viewers exclusively with Israeli troops framed as helpless victims, while the Palestinian other stays faceless, voiceless, and objectified (the staggering Lebanese woman, the trauma displaced onto dead dogs and horses). Drawing on Judith Butler's frames of war and "ungrievable" lives, he reads this as Kimmerling's latent cognitive militarism that denies the enemy's competing subjectivity and forecloses nonviolent alternatives.

chapters.file: ch20 - General Patton and Private Ryan The Conflicting Reality of War and Films about War.md
chapters.relation: Fiala uses Patton's opening speech ("an army is a team… this individuality stuff is a bunch of crap") against Saving Private Ryan's mission to rescue one soldier to frame war's basic conflict between the collective and the individual, and to expose the problem of "realism" in representing war. He aligns the collectivist realist ethics of war against the just-war tradition's deontological respect for individuals as Kantian ends-in-themselves, and contrasts Patton's aerial, above-the-battle viewpoint with Private Ryan's first-person D-Day realism. Drawing on Tim O'Brien's claim that a true war story is never moral, and on Nussbaum's and Glover's moral imagination, he concludes that no film can synthesize war's public and private perspectives—mirroring the failure of moral imagination that produces war itself.

holes.name: Aspect Perception (seeing-as)
holes.what: Wittgenstein's concept from Philosophical Investigations II.xi of seeing one thing as another (the duck-rabbit), and the ethical articulation of experience it can involve.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument turns on aspect perception / 'seeing as' as an interpretive and ethical concept, which the taxonomy's Wittgenstein concepts (language-games, private-language) do not capture.

holes.name: Privileged Access (the perceptual model of self-knowledge)
holes.what: The view that a subject has direct, asymmetric introspective access to private inner mental states unavailable to others, modeling self-knowledge on inner perception.
holes.why: Chapter 14's central philosophical target is the 'privileged access' / perceptual model of self-knowledge that Apocalypse Now is read as dismantling, and no taxonomy concept names this doctrine of self-knowledge.

holes.name: Grievability / Frames of War
holes.what: Judith Butler's idea that normative frames determine whose lives are recognized as grievable and whose deaths are rendered ungrievable and thus outside the field of moral concern.
holes.why: Chapter 19 explicitly builds its critique of the 'ubiquitously absent enemy' on Butler's frames of war and ungrievable lives, and the taxonomy has no Butler concept beyond gender-performativity/heteronormativity.
